measures.name: Text out of the head
measures.conversion: Characters a minute are shown as words at five characters a word, the convention typing speed is measured by (so 90 characters a minute is shown as 18 words a minute, which is also how the 2023 Stanford paper restates the 2021 figure).
measures.meaning: How fast a person produced text through a brain link, in words or characters a minute as the paper gave it, with the vocabulary and the error rate beside it. A high rate with a small vocabulary or a high error rate is not the same thing as a high rate with neither; the table says which is which.

points.what: Copy typing on an on-screen keyboard by cursor control: 39.2 correct characters a minute (the paper's own 7.8 words a minute) for participant T5 with an optimised keyboard layout; 31.6 for T6 and 13.5 for T7. Free typing by T6 ran at 24.4 correct characters a minute over three days.
points.who: Chethan Pandarinath, Paul Nuyujukian and colleagues at Stanford (Krishna Shenoy and Jaimie Henderson, senior authors), in the BrainGate2 pilot trial.
points.in_whom: Three people with paralysis: T6, a woman of 51 with motor neurone disease; T5, a man of 63 with tetraplegia from a spinal cord injury; T7, a man of 54 with motor neurone disease.
points.repeated: Three participants, over two to five days each; the paper reports every one. The 39.2 figure is T5's average, not a one-off peak.
points.source_note: eLife 6:e18554, published 2017-02-21. The Results give the per-participant figures; the Discussion restates them as 6.3, 7.8 and 2.7 words a minute.

upgrade.name: A wired brain implant lets a paralysed person control a cursor

points.what: Attempted handwriting decoded into text: 90 characters a minute with 94.1 per cent raw accuracy online, and above 99 per cent offline with a general-purpose autocorrect. The paper compares it with smartphone typing in the participant's age group, 115 characters a minute. As errors: one character in seventeen wrong (5.9 per cent across the five test days, 5.4 on the last, where the speed levelled off at 90) and one word in four (25.1 per cent) as decoded live, falling to 0.89 per cent of characters and 3.4 per cent of words with the autocorrect applied afterwards. Writing his own answers to questions rather than copying, he reached 73.8 characters a minute.
points.who: Francis Willett and colleagues at Stanford (Jaimie Henderson and Krishna Shenoy, senior authors), in the BrainGate2 pilot trial.
points.in_whom: One man, T5, paralysed from the neck down by a spinal cord injury.
points.repeated: A single participant, tested on five days of copying sentences and two of free answers; the paper calls it a proof of concept in one person and says more work is needed to show it in others.
points.source_note: Nature 593, pages 249 to 254, published 2021-05-12. The 90, 94.1, 99 and 115 figures are in the abstract; the error rates are in the Results and its Table 1, the free-typing figures in the Results. Full text read on 2026-10-20.

upgrade.name: A wired brain implant lets a paralysed person control a cursor

points.what: Attempted speech decoded into text: 62 words a minute, with a 23.8 per cent word error rate on a 125,000-word vocabulary and 9.1 per cent on a 50-word vocabulary. The paper calls it 3.4 times the previous record and says it begins to approach the speed of natural conversation, which it puts at 160 words a minute.
points.who: Francis Willett, Erin Kunz, Chaofei Fan and colleagues at Stanford (Jaimie Henderson, senior author), in the BrainGate2 pilot trial.
points.in_whom: One woman, T12, aged 67 during the study, with motor neurone disease that began in the muscles of speech about nine years before she enrolled, unable to produce intelligible speech.
points.repeated: A single participant, over five days of attempted speech aloud and three of silent attempts; the paper says the results must be confirmed in more people.
points.source_note: Nature 620, pages 1031 to 1036, published 2023-08-23; the figures are in the abstract and the Results (Table 1), the participant's age and sex in the paper's reporting summary. Full text read on 2026-10-20. The paper itself says a word error rate near 24 per cent is probably not yet low enough for everyday use.

upgrade.name: A brain implant turns intended speech into text at conversational speed

points.what: Silently attempted speech decoded into text, speech sounds and a talking avatar: a median of 78 words a minute (78.3 in the main text) with a median word error rate of 25 per cent (25.5), on a vocabulary of 1,024 words, from high-density recordings on the surface of the speech cortex. The paper calls this large-vocabulary decoding; the 1,024 words are those of the sentences used to test it (249 sentences, not used in training), and a larger vocabulary of 39,378 words was tried only offline, at a word error rate of 27.6 per cent.
points.who: Sean Metzger, Kaylo Littlejohn, Alexander Silva, David Moses, Margaret Seaton and colleagues at the University of California, San Francisco (Edward Chang, senior author).
points.in_whom: One woman, the trial's participant Bravo-3, with severe limb and vocal paralysis.
points.repeated: A single participant; the paper's readable text makes no claim of repetition.
points.source_note: Nature 620, pages 1037 to 1046, published 2023-08-23. The 78 words a minute and 25 per cent figures are in the abstract. The vocabulary is read from the full text (open copy, PubMed Central PMC10826467, and the journal's page, both read on 2026-10-17): the legend of Figure 2 says its panels, including the decoded words a minute, "were computed using the real-time evaluation trials with the 1024-word-General sentence set"; the text of the Results gives the median rate as 78.3 words a minute and the median word error rate as 25.5 per cent on those trials, and says the sentences were 249 drawn at random from that set, not used in training. The sentence that gives 78.3 follows one about a freeform test, and the text cites its figure panel as 2f where the legend labels the decoded-rate panel 2e; the legend's statement that panels b to g were computed on the 1024-word real-time trials is what ties the rate to that vocabulary.

upgrade.name: A brain implant turns intended speech into text at conversational speed

points.what: Attempted speech decoded into text at the participant's own pace: 31.6 words a minute with a 2.5 per cent word error rate on a vocabulary of over 125,000 words, sustained at 97.5 per cent accuracy over 248 hours of use across eight months. Slower than the 2023 decoders and far more accurate; included because the series records every demonstrated figure, not only the records.
points.who: Nicholas Card, Sergey Stavisky, David Brandman and colleagues at the University of California, Davis, in the BrainGate2 pilot trial.
points.in_whom: One man of 45 with motor neurone disease and severe speech impairment, with four 64-electrode arrays (256 electrodes) in the left precentral gyrus.
points.repeated: A single participant, over 84 research sessions and eight months; the accuracy held across them.
points.source_note: New England Journal of Medicine 391, pages 609 to 618; published online 2024-08-14 and dated 2024-08-15 in the print issue (the date given is the first). The 31.6 words a minute and 2.5 per cent figures are in the Results, the 97.5 per cent and 125,000 in the abstract. The online day rests on UC Davis Health's own release of 2024-08-14, which says the study "was published today" in the journal (https://health.ucdavis.edu/news/headlines/new-brain-computer-interface-allows-man-with-als-to-speak-again/2024/08), and agrees with the PubMed record (entered 2024-08-14, print date 2024-08-15) and the DOI registry (record created 2024-08-14). The journal's own page sits behind a bot check that was not bypassed.

upgrade.name: A brain implant turns intended speech into text at conversational speed

points.what: Attempted speech decoded into text in everyday life at home, with no researcher present: an average of 56 words a minute across 183,060 sentences (1,960,163 words) over nearly two years, from a vocabulary of over 125,000 words. The accuracy of that everyday use was rated by the participant himself, sentence by sentence: he marked 92 per cent at least mostly right and 53.3 per cent exactly right. When he repeated sentences shown on a screen, so that errors could be counted, the decoder was right on more than 99 per cent of words at 30.6 words a minute speaking aloud and 96.5 per cent at 49.7 words a minute speaking silently. The same implant also moved a computer cursor, at 2.90 bits a second on the grid task.
points.who: Nicholas Card, Sergey Stavisky, David Brandman and colleagues at the University of California, Davis, in the BrainGate2 pilot trial.
points.in_whom: The same man as the 2024 point, T15, who has motor neurone disease and was 45 when he enrolled in 2023; four 64-electrode arrays in the speech area of the left side of the brain, wired through the skin.
points.repeated: A single participant, who used it for more than 3,800 hours on 444 of 653 days; the paper says it is not yet known whether the results carry over to other people.
points.source_note: Nature Medicine 32, pages 2504 to 2510, published online 2026-06-15. The 56 words a minute, the sentence and word counts, the 92 per cent and the 125,000 words are in the abstract; the 53.3 per cent, the copy-task figures and the cursor rate are in the Results. Full text read on 2026-10-20. The paper notes that accuracy in his own conversation was not as consistently high as on prompted sentences, and that the system needed daily setup by trained carers and could not leave the house.

upgrade.name: A brain implant turns intended speech into text at conversational speed

points.note: Slower than the 2023 decoders. Its place in the series is that, to its authors' knowledge, it is the first speech implant used independently at home, here for nearly two years. The 56 words a minute is plotted; its accuracy rests on the participant's own ratings, not a count of errors, so it is not the same kind of figure as the others on this measure.

baselines.label: Speech in conversation
baselines.who: The rate the 2023 Stanford speech paper gives for natural conversation, citing a 2006 study of conversational speaking rate by Jiahong Yuan, Mark Liberman and Christopher Cieri.
baselines.source_note: Willett and colleagues, Nature 2023, abstract: "begins to approach the speed of natural conversation (160 words per minute)", with the citation to Yuan, Liberman and Cieri, Interspeech 2006 (DOI 10.21437/Interspeech.2006-204).

baselines.label: A fast typist
baselines.who: The rate Jieyu Zheng and Markus Meister (California Institute of Technology) give for an advanced typist working from a manuscript, in their 2024 analysis of the speed of human behaviour.
baselines.source_note: Zheng and Meister, Neuron, published online 2024-12-17: "An advanced typist produces 120 words per minute", which they put at about 10 bits a second.

baselines.label: Typing on a phone
baselines.who: The rate the 2021 Stanford handwriting paper gives for smartphone typing by people in its participant's age group.
baselines.source_note: Willett and colleagues, Nature 2021, abstract: "typical smartphone typing speeds of individuals in the age group of our participant (115 characters per minute)".

measures.name: Pointing at a screen
measures.meaning: How much information a person's cursor control carried, in bits a second, measured by the field's grid task: targets appear on a grid, the person moves to and selects them, and the rate counts how many right selections were made per second against how many targets there were to choose from. It measures pointing, not language, so a figure here is not comparable to a figure for text.

points.what: The first BrainGate participant moving a cursor, opening simulated e-mail and operating a television through a 96-electrode array in the part of the brain that plans hand movement. The paper states no rate: no bits a second, no characters a minute.
points.who: Leigh Hochberg and colleagues at Massachusetts General Hospital and Brown University, with Cyberkinetics Neurotechnology Systems (John Donoghue, senior author).
points.in_whom: A tetraplegic man, MN (Matt Nagle), three years after a spinal cord injury.
points.repeated: The paper's readable text makes no claim of repetition; a supplementary video names a second trial participant, but the text does not report his results.
points.source_note: Nature 442, pages 164 to 171, published 2006-07-13. The abstract names the 96-microelectrode array and describes the neural cursor; it gives no rate.

upgrade.name: A wired brain implant lets a paralysed person control a cursor

points.note: Here as the series' starting mark: the first hundred-electrode implant in a person, from which every later point descends. The implant date (June 2004) is not in the paper's readable text and is not stated here.

points.what: Cursor control on a grid task: 4.16 bits a second for participant T5 on a 9 by 9 grid, which the paper calls, to its authors' knowledge, the highest documented brain-computer interface communication rate for a person with motor impairment. On the 6 by 6 grid the averages were 2.2 (T6), 3.7 (T5) and 1.4 (T7) bits a second.
points.who: Chethan Pandarinath, Paul Nuyujukian and colleagues at Stanford (Krishna Shenoy and Jaimie Henderson, senior authors), in the BrainGate2 pilot trial.
points.in_whom: Three people with paralysis: T6, T5 and T7, as above; the 4.16 figure is T5's.
points.repeated: Three participants over two to five days each; the 4.16 figure is one participant's average over his sessions on the denser grid.

upgrade.name: A wired brain implant lets a paralysed person control a cursor

points.what: Cursor control on the company's grid task: 8.0 bits a second, after a first-session figure of 4.6 that the company called a new world record for human brain-computer interface cursor control. The post says he was trying to beat the company's engineers using a mouse, about 10 bits a second. A later post (2024-08-21) says his performance has since more than doubled the prior record, without a new number.
points.who: Neuralink, in its own progress post; measured by the company, not in a peer-reviewed paper.
points.in_whom: One man, Noland Arbaugh, the first participant in the company's PRIME trial, paralysed below the shoulders by a spinal cord injury; the implant has 1,024 electrodes on 64 threads.
points.repeated: A single participant with a stated figure. The company's 2024-08-21 post says a second participant, Alex, broke the previous record with another company's device on his first day, with no figure given.
points.source_note: Neuralink, "PRIME Study Progress Update, User Experience", 2024-05-08, the section headed BCI Use. The same post says threads retracted from the brain in the weeks after surgery, cutting the rate until the software was changed.

upgrade.name: A fully implanted wireless brain chip lets a paralysed person control a computer

baselines.label: Engineers with a mouse
baselines.who: Neuralink's own figure for its engineers using a mouse on the same grid task, about 10 bits a second.
baselines.source_note: Neuralink, 2024-05-08: "currently trying to beat scores of the Neuralink engineers using a mouse (~10 BPS)".

baselines.label: Speech, as information
baselines.who: The information rate of speech across 17 languages, measured by Christophe Coupé, Yoon Mi Oh, Dan Dediu and François Pellegrino (CNRS and the University of Lyon) in 170 speakers reading texts aloud: a mean of 39.15 bits a second. Shown here because it is the number the merger argument compares a brain link against; it is a rate of language, not of pointing.
baselines.source_note: Science Advances 5, eaaw2594, published 2019-09-04: "languages encoding similar information rates (~39 bits/s)"; Results give 39.15 bits a second with a standard deviation of 5.10.
